_comment: Michael Dickens, "Where I Am Donating in 2025", snapshotted by scripts/fetch-mdickens-reviews.ts. Each body opens with his classification of the org, then his write-up, then his top-five prioritization note or donation reasoning where there is one.

reviews.classification: Tax-deductible; deserves more funding, but not one of my top candidates this year
reviews.review:
Classification: Tax-deductible; deserves more funding, but not one of my top candidates this year

The AI Safety and Governance Fund does [message testing](https://manifund.org/projects/testing-and-spreading-messages-to-reduce-ai-x-risk)) on what sorts of AI safety messaging people found compelling. More recently, they [created a chatbot](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/w5tzAyRxdGhHfvxxB/we-ve-automated-x-risk-pilling-people) that talks about AI x-risk, which they use to feed into their messaging experiments; they also have [plans](https://aisgf.us/fundraising) for new activities they could pursue with additional funding.

I liked AI Safety and Governance Fund’s original project, and I donated $10,000 because I expected they could do a lot of message testing for not much money. I’m more uncertain about its new project, or how well message testing can scale. I’m optimistic, but not optimistic enough for the org to be one of my top donation candidates, so I’m not donating more this year.

reviews.classification: Tax-deductible; deserves more funding, but not one of my top candidates
reviews.review:
Classification: Tax-deductible; deserves more funding, but not one of my top candidates

[Existential Risk Observatory](https://www.existentialriskobservatory.org/) writes [media articles](https://www.existentialriskobservatory.org/#in-the-media) on AI x-risk, does [policy research](https://www.existentialriskobservatory.org/research-2/), and publishes [policy proposals](https://www.existentialriskobservatory.org/policy-proposals/) (see [pdf](https://existentialriskobservatory.org/papers_and_reports/Policy%20Proposals.pdf) with a summary of proposals).

Last year, I [wrote](https://mdickens.me/2024/11/18/where_i_am_donating_in_2024/#existential-risk-observatory):

> My primary concern is that it operates in the Netherlands. Dutch policy is unlikely to have much influence on x-risk—the United States is the most important country by far, followed by China. And a Dutch organization likely has little influence on United States policy. Existential Risk Observatory can still influence public opinion in America (for example via its TIME article), but I expect a US-headquartered org to have a greater impact.

I’m less concerned about that now—I believe I gave too little weight to the fact that Existential Risk Observatory has published articles in international media outlets.

I still like media outreach as a form of impact, but it’s not my *favorite* thing, so Existential Risk Observatory is not one of my top candidates.

Classification: Tax-deductible; deserves more funding

The biggest news from [MIRI](https://intelligence.org/) in 2025 is that they [published a book](https://ifanyonebuildsit.com/). The book was widely read and got some [endorsements](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/khmpWJnGJnuyPdipE/new-endorsements-for-if-anyone-builds-it-everyone-dies) from important people, including people who I wouldn’t have expected to give endorsements. It remains to be seen what sort of lasting impact the book will have, but the launch went better than I would’ve predicted a year ago (perhaps in the 75th percentile).

MIRI’s 2026 plans include:

- growing the comms team and continuing to promote the book;
- talking to policy-makers, think tanks, etc. about AI x-risk;
- growing the Technical Governance team, which does policy research on how to implement a global ban on ASI.

I’m less enthusiastic about policy research than about advocacy, but I like MIRI’s approach to policy research better than any other org’s. Most AI policy orgs take an academia-style approach of “what are some novel things we can publish about AI policy?” MIRI takes a more motivated approach of “what policies are necessary to prevent extinction, and what needs to happen before those policies can be implemented?” Most policy research orgs spend too much time on [streetlight-effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetlight_effect) policies; MIRI is strongly oriented toward preventing extinction.

I also like MIRI better than I did a year ago because I realized they deserve a “stable preference bonus”.

In [My Cause Selection (2015)](https://mdickens.me/2015/09/15/my_cause_selection/), MIRI was my #2 choice for where to donate. In 2024, MIRI again made my list of finalists. The fact that I’ve liked MIRI for 10 years is good evidence that I’ll continue to like it.

Maybe next year I will change my mind about my other top candidates, but—according to the [Lindy effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindy_effect)—I bet I won’t change my mind about MIRI.

The Survival & Flourishing Fund is [matching](https://survivalandflourishing.fund/2025/recommendations) 2025 donations to MIRI up to $1.3 million.

reviews.classification: Tax-deductible; one of my favorite AI safety nonprofits
reviews.review:
Classification: Tax-deductible; one of my favorite AI safety nonprofits

[Palisade](https://palisaderesearch.org/) builds demonstrations of the offensive capabilities of AI systems, with the goal of illustrating risks to policy-makers. My opinion on Palisade is mostly unchanged since [last year](https://mdickens.me/2024/11/18/where_i_am_donating_in_2024/#palisade-research), which is to say it’s one of my favorite AI safety nonprofits.

They did not respond to my emails asking about their fundraising situation. Palisade did recently receive funding from the Survival & Flourishing Fund (SFF) and appeared on their [Further Opportunities page](https://survivalandflourishing.fund/2025/further-opportunities), which means SFF thinks Palisade can productively use more funding.

The Survival & Flourishing Fund is [matching](https://survivalandflourishing.fund/2025/recommendations) 2025 donations to Palisade up to $900,000.

Classification: Favorite tax-deductible donation target; donating $40,000

[PauseAI US](https://www.pauseai-us.org/) was the main place I donated last year. Since then, I’ve become [more optimistic](https://mdickens.me/2025/04/18/protest_outcomes_critical_review/) that protests are net positive.

Pause protests haven’t had any big visible effects in the last year, which is what I expected, but it’s a weak negative update that the protests haven’t yet gotten traction.

I did not list protests as one of my [favorite interventions](https://mdickens.me/2025/11/22/where_i_am_donating_in_2025/#my-favorite-interventions); in the abstract, I like political advocacy better. But political advocacy is more difficult to evaluate, operates in a more adversarial information environment, and less neglected. There is some hypothetical political advocacy that I like better than protests, but it’s much harder to tell whether the real-life opportunities live up to that hypothetical.

PauseAI US has hired a full-time lobbyist. He’s less experienced than the lobbyists at some other AI safety orgs, but I know that his lobbying efforts straightforwardly focus on x-risk instead of doing some kind of complicated political maneuvering that’s hard for me to evaluate, like what some other orgs do. PauseAI US has had some early successes but it’s hard for me to judge how important they are.

Something that didn’t occur to me last year, but that I now believe matters a lot, is that PauseAI US organizes letter-writing campaigns. In May, PauseAI US [organized a campaign](https://pauseaius.substack.com/p/call-to-action-contact-your-senators) to ask Congress members not to impose a 10-year moratorium on AI regulation; they have an [ongoing campaign](https://pauseai-us.org/RiskEvalAct) in support of the AI Risk Evaluation Act. According to my recent [cost-effectiveness analysis](https://mdickens.me/2025/11/08/call_or_write_your_representatives/), messaging campaigns look valuable, and right now nobody else is doing it. It could be that these campaigns are the most important function of PauseAI US.

All of the orgs on my 501(c)(3) list deserve more funding. (I suspect the same is true of the 501(c)(4)s, but I’m not confident.) **My favorite 501(c)(3) donation target is PauseAI US** because:

- Someone should be organizing protests. The only US-based orgs doing that are PauseAI US and Stop AI, and I have some concerns about Stop AI that I discussed [last year](https://mdickens.me/2024/11/18/where_i_am_donating_in_2024/#stop-ai) and [above](https://mdickens.me/2025/11/22/where_i_am_donating_in_2025/#peaceful-protests-probably-help).
- Someone should be running messaging campaigns to support good legislation and oppose bad legislation. Only PauseAI US is doing that.
- PauseAI US is small and doesn’t get much funding, and in particular doesn’t get support from any grantmakers.

In other words, PauseAI US is serving some important functions that nobody else is on top of, and I really want them to be able to keep doing that.

My plan is to donate $40,000 to PauseAI US.

Classification: Non-tax-deductible; open questions, no position yet

[AI Policy Network](https://theaipn.org/) advocates for US Congress to pass AI safety regulation. From its description of [The Issue](https://theaipn.org/the-issue/), it appears appropriately concerned about misalignment risk, but it also says

> AGI would further have large implications for national security and the balance of power. If an adversarial nation beats the U.S. to AGI, they could potentially use the power it would provide – in technological advancement, economic activity, and geopolitical strategy – to reshape the world order against U.S. interests.

I find this sort of language concerning because it appears to be encouraging an arms race, although I don’t think that’s what the writers of this paragraph want.

I don’t have a good understanding of what AI Policy Network does, so I need to learn more.

reviews.classification: Non-tax-deductible; open questions, no position yet
reviews.review:
Classification: Non-tax-deductible; open questions, no position yet

[Americans for Responsible Innovation](https://ari.us/) (ARI) is the sort of respectable-looking org that I don’t expect to struggle for funding. But I spoke to someone at ARI who believes that the best donation opportunities depend on small donors because there are legal donation caps. Even if the org as a whole is well-funded, it depends on small donors to fund its [PAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committee).

I want to put more thought into how valuable ARI’s activities are, but I haven’t had time to do that yet. My outstanding questions:

- How cost-effective is ARI’s advocacy (e.g. compared to [messaging campaigns](https://mdickens.me/2025/11/08/call_or_write_your_representatives/))? (I have weak reason to believe it’s more cost-effective.)
- How much do I agree with ARI’s policy objectives, and how much should I trust them?
- ARI is pretty opaque about what they do. How concerned should I be about that?

reviews.review:
Classification: Non-tax-deductible; tentatively my favorite non-tax-deductible org

[ControlAI](https://mdickens.me/controlai.com/) is the most x-risk-focused of the 501(c)(4)s, and the only one that advocates for a pause on AI development. They started operations in the UK, and this year they have [expanded to the US](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/Xwrajm92fdjd7cqnN/what-we-learned-from-briefing-70-lawmakers-on-the-threat?commentId=fBZuzesMbtpA6B5tF).

Some thoughts:

- ControlAI’s [open letter](https://aitreaty.org/) calling for an international treaty looks eminently reasonable.
- ControlAI had success getting UK politicians to [support](https://controlai.com/statement#supporters) their statement on AI risk.
- They wrote a [LessWrong post](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/Xwrajm92fdjd7cqnN/what-we-learned-from-briefing-70-lawmakers-on-the-threat) about what they learned from talking to policy-makers about AI risk, which was a valuable post that demonstrated thoughtfulness.
- I liked ControlAI [last year](https://mdickens.me/2024/11/18/where_i_am_donating_in_2024/#control-ai), but at the time they only operated in the UK, so they weren’t a finalist. This year they are expanding internationally.

ControlAI is tentatively my favorite non-tax-deductible org because they’re the most transparent and the most focused on x-risk.

Classification: Non-tax-deductible; open questions, no position yet

[Encode](https://encodeai.org/what-we-do/) does political advocacy on AI x-risk. They also have [local chapters](https://encodeai.org/our-chapters/) that do something (I’m not clear on what).

They have a good track record of political action:

- Encode co-sponsored SB 1047 and the new [SB 53](https://sd11.senate.ca.gov/news/senator-wiener-introduces-legislation-protect-ai-whistleblowers-boost-responsible-ai).
- Encode filed in support of Musk’s lawsuit against OpenAI’s for-profit conversion, which was the [largest theft in human history](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/wCc7XDbD8LdaHwbYg/openai-moves-to-complete-potentially-the-largest-theft-in).

Encode is relatively transparent and relatively focused on the big problems, although not to the same extent as ControlAI.
